means:
**Adj.:** (1) belonging to the **same time** as something else; (2) belonging to **the present** — modern, current.
**Noun:** a person living at the same time as another — *Leibniz was a contemporary of Newton*.

Sense (1) is the one the GRE tests, and it's relational: contemporary *with* or *of* something. So "**contemporary accounts** of the battle" means written by people who were there — not written by modern historians. When the word stands alone with no comparison point ("contemporary art", "contemporary dance"), the era it matches is *ours*. Same word, two clocks: it always means "of that time," and context decides which time.
trap: ⚠️ **contemporary ≠ contemporaneous.** *Contemporaneous* only ever means "happening at the same time," usually of events or documents (*contemporaneous notes*) — it can never mean "modern." Anything described as contemporaneous is being dated, not praised as current.
trick_line: **Contemporary** hides **tempo** — two things keeping the *same tempo* are running on the same clock.
trick_unpack: The buried *tempo* pulls you to the "same era as" sense rather than the lazy "modern" reading.
sentences: Scholars prize the diary because it is **contemporary** with the siege itself, not a reconstruction written forty years later.
My gran and Elvis were **contemporaries**, which she brings up roughly once a week.
in_the_wild: A **Museum of Contemporary Art** shows work by artists who are alive now — the label is a date range, not a style.
etymology:
Latin **con-** (*together*) + **tempus, temporis** (*time*) — literally "sharing a time."

That root pays off everywhere: **temporary** (lasting a short time), **temporal** (of time, or of the worldly world as opposed to the eternal), **tempo**, **extempore** (out of the moment, unprepared), **temporize** (stall for time).
one_line: Of the same era as; or belonging to the present day.
